## July 28, 2026

In this post, I'm prototyping a page about bridging
the gap between undergraduate calculus and research
in Yang Mills quantum gauge theory. 

The motivation for this page is to help me overcome 
my lack of confidence in my calculus knowledge, which 
frequently causes me strife in my research into 
Yang Mills quantum gauge theory. The idea is to find a better solution
than the following two reactions to this problem. 
The first reaction is to give up entirely 
on research into Yang Mills quantum gauge theory
and focus purely on undergraduate level calculus. 
The second reaction is to deny that I lack some 
foundational knowledge in calculus, and press forward 
with increasing psychological strife into 
the modern papers on Yang Mills quantum theory.

So my proposed solution is to find 
logical statements in modern papers on Yang Mills theory
whose proofs or derivations are treatable
with undergrad level calculus, after unraveling the 
definitions. 

Let me begin with an example. 

### Problem 1. 
This problem comes from the section on 
the $\phi^4_2$ model in @BrenneckeCQFT.

Suppose 
$f, g \in D(\mathbb T^2) = 
\{f \in C^\infty(\R^2, \C): f(x + k) = f(x) \forall k \in \Z^2 \}$.
Show that 
$$
\left \langle f, \frac{1}{-\Delta + m^2} g 
\right \rangle_{L^2(\mathbb T^2, \C)}
= 
\sum_{p \in 2\pi \Z^2} \frac{\overline{\hat{f}}(p) \hat{g}(p) }{|p|^2 + m^2}.
$$

The formula, based on spectral calculus, for 
$\frac{1}{-\Delta + m^2} g$ is 
$$
(\frac{1}{-\Delta + m^2} g) (p) =
\left( \mathcal{F}^{-1} \circ \left[ \frac{1}{|\cdot|^2 + m^2} 
\right] \circ \mathcal{F} \right) (p)
$$
where 
$$
(\mathcal{F}f)(p) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}} \int_{\R^d}
$$

I'm tempted to make a foray into Fourier theory
after checking some course notes online. It looks to be
a subject full of calculus problems.
